newsitem.title: USA: Judge says will rule later on Marvel case.
newsitem.headline: Judge says will rule later on Marvel case.

text.p: A judge in Delaware said he will rule later on whether to lift a restraining order that prevents holders of Marvel Holdings Inc from voting the 80 percent stake in Marvel Entertainment that secures nearly $900 million in bond debt.

But in a two-hour hearing, Judge Roderick McKelvie of the U.S. District Court in Delaware repeatedly told attornies of Marvel, its banks and bondholders that if bondholders had the right to foreclose on their shares, they should have the right to vote them.

"It's radically inconsistent with law to say bondholders can't seat directors, because you anticipate a decision that will not be in the best interest of the estate. Let them take their seat, then review any decision that is not in the best interest of the estate," McKelvie said.

An attorney for Chase Manhattan Corp -- a secured creditor of Marvel -- said, "If (investor) Carl Icahn (leader of the bondholder group) and his crowd get control, this business may go into free-fall, and if his honor doesn't sustain the (restraining order), it could happen tomorrow."
The judge responded that, "Any order I enter isn't going to allow for a free-fall" until a June 16 hearing scheduled before a bankruptcy court on the issue.
"I just don't think the order to stay (the restraining order) is the right one."

At issue are two decisions by U.S. bankruptcy court Judge Helen Balick. In February, she ruled that bondholders could foreclose on the shares securing their debt. But in late March, she granted Marvel a restraining order that prevented the bondholders from voting those shares to replace Marvel's board, as they had indicated they would do.
McKelvie said, "I think the second decision is clearly wrong as a matter of law."
An attorney for the public stockholders of Marvel asked the judge to lift the restraining order, saying "Marvel's current board has been hostile to public stockholders."
He noted that because the company owes about $900 million to bondholders and $700 million to banks, "Ronald Perelman doesn't get a cent out of this company until $1.6 billion in debt is paid."

The bondholder group earlier this week filed a reorganization plan in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware, which includes a $365 million rights offering. The plan also proposed the creation of a transition team to resuscitate the company, which would be led by former Marvel executive Joseph Calamari, according to the bondholders.

The filing came one day after financier Perelman and Marvel's bankers, including Chase Manhattan, reached a deal to sell Marvel's comic book and entertainment operations to Toy Biz Inc, which is controlled by Isaac Perlmutter.
"We think you should exercise your authority on a crucial corporate governance issue and revoke the restraining order immediately," the stockholder attorney told McKelvie.

In response, the attorney for Chase Manhattan said "This company is insolvent and hopelessly so." He supported his claim by citing a Bear Stearns' mid-range valuation for Marvel of negative $137 million. The high-end of that range was negative $67 million. "With this valuation of the company, the real parties in interest are the creditors, not the shareholders," the bank's attorney said.
The banks are secured creditors. The debt owned by the bondholders is secured by shares of Marvel Entertainment.
